Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Wife and servant are the same, But only differ in the name: For when that fatal knot is tied, Which nothing, nothing can divide: When she the word obey has said, And man by law supreme has made, Then all that’s kind is laid aside, And nothing left but state and pride: Fierce as an Eastern prince he grows, And all his innate rigour shows: Then but to look, to laugh, or speak, Will the nuptial contract break. Like mutes she signs alone must make, And never any freedom take: But still be governed by a nod, And fear her husband as a God: Him still must serve, him still obey, And nothing act, and nothing say, But what her haughty lord thinks fit, Who with the power, has all the wit. Then shun, oh! shun that wretched state, And all the fawning flatt’rers hate: Value your selves, and men despise, You must be proud, if you’ll be wise.

Here is a paraphrase of the text, preserving its meaning while using fresh wording and structure:

A wife holds no different position than a servant—only the title distinguishes them. Once the irreversible bond of marriage is sealed, she speaks her vow of obedience, and the law elevates her husband to a position of complete authority. From that moment, tenderness vanishes entirely, replaced solely by dominance and arrogance. He transforms into something like a tyrannical ruler, revealing the harshness that was always within him. The smallest gesture on her part—a glance, a smile, a single word—becomes enough to shatter their marital agreement.

Like someone forced into silence, she may only communicate through gestures, forbidden any independence. Her existence becomes dictated by his slightest signal, and she must revere him as though he were divine. She exists only to attend to him and follow his commands, permitted no thought or speech beyond what pleases her domineering master—a man who, holding all the power, is assumed to possess all wisdom as well.

Therefore, women should flee from this miserable condition and reject those who would flatter them into it. Hold yourselves in high regard, and look upon men with skepticism; wisdom, for a woman, requires a measure of pride.

**On the Illusion of Marriage: A Critique**

There exists, in the eyes of many who have looked closely at the institution of matrimony, little meaningful distinction between the role of a wife and that of a servant. Both are bound by duty, both are expected to obey, and both find their identities subsumed beneath the will of another. The only difference, some would argue, lies in the title bestowed upon them—"wife" carrying a veneer of romantic legitimacy that "servant" does not. Yet beneath this veneer, the practical reality remains the same: a woman who marries enters into a bond that, once sealed, cannot be undone, a contract as binding and inescapable as any indenture.

The transformation that follows the wedding vow is, in this view, swift and stark. The moment a woman utters the word "obey" before witnesses and the law affixes its seal to the union, something shifts irrevocably. The husband who once wooed her with tenderness, who once seemed gentle and accommodating in his courtship, sheds that gentleness like an outgrown garment. In its place emerges dominance, entitlement, and a quiet but unmistakable pride—as though the very act of marriage has granted him ownership rather than partnership.

This shift in temperament often escalates into something resembling tyranny. The husband, once a suitor eager to please, becomes akin to an "Eastern prince" ruling over a private domain where his word is absolute law. Within this domain, even the smallest and most innocent of actions—an unguarded glance, a moment of laughter shared with another, an unsolicited word spoken freely—can be construed as transgressions, as violations of an unspoken contract of submission. The wife's every movement becomes subject to scrutiny, her spontaneity a liability.

Under such conditions, the wife is gradually stripped of her voice and her agency. She learns to communicate not through words but through silent gestures, much like one who has been rendered mute—not by physical affliction, but by the social and emotional constraints placed upon her. Freedom, once perhaps only partially hers, evaporates entirely. She comes to live in a state of perpetual vigilance and fear, treating her husband's moods and judgments with the reverence and terror one might reserve for a deity, rather than the mutual respect one would expect between equal partners.

Given this bleak portrayal, women are urged to think critically before entering into such an arrangement. They are encouraged to see through the flattering words of suitors, which often mask the reality of what marriage may become. Instead of seeking validation through romantic pursuit or societal expectation, women are called to recognize their own inherent worth, independent of a husband's approval or a marital title. Pride, in this context, is reframed not as a vice but as a form of wisdom—a necessary armor against subjugation, and a declaration that one's dignity need not be surrendered at the altar.

# Expanding the Summary into a Full Analysis

The poem confronts the institution of marriage as a site of profound inequality, stripping away romantic illusions to reveal the harsh realities that await women who enter into it. Through the poet's use of vivid, often visceral imagery, marriage is depicted not as a union of equals but as a form of bondage—one that transforms a once-independent woman into something akin to a domestic servant. The vows exchanged at the altar, rather than symbolizing mutual devotion, become chains: unbreakable commitments that bind the wife to obedience while granting the husband near-total authority over her life, body, and choices. This asymmetry is rendered starkly through direct address, as the speaker turns outward to confront the reader—likely a female audience—urging them to see clearly what marriage actually demands of them, rather than what society claims it offers.

The poem's language emphasizes confinement and diminishment. Where a husband is cast as an authoritarian figure, the wife is reduced to a role defined by service and submission, her identity subsumed beneath domestic duty and spousal command. The imagery reinforces this power imbalance, using metaphors of servitude, restriction, and control to illustrate how the "wretched state" of marriage erodes a woman's autonomy and self-worth. There is no room in this depiction for partnership or affection; instead, the poem insists that marriage as an institution is structurally designed to benefit men at women's expense.

Yet the poem does not stop at critique—it moves toward a call to action. Its central message urges women to reject this "wretched state" outright, refusing to accept subjugation as their inevitable fate. Rather than internalizing the submissiveness that marriage demands, women are encouraged to recognize and value their own worth, to see themselves as deserving of respect and autonomy rather than servitude. The poem explicitly champions pride over submission, framing self-respect not as arrogance but as a necessary form of resistance against a system designed to diminish women.

In this sense, the poem functions as an early feminist manifesto, articulating ideas that would only be fully developed centuries later. By naming the mechanisms of oppression within marriage—the vows, the authority structures, the erasure of female autonomy—the poem gives voice to a critique of patriarchal norms well before such critiques became mainstream. Its insistence that women resist these norms, assert their own value, and embrace pride rather than compliance positions it as a powerful, if historically underappreciated, contribution to the long tradition of feminist thought and resistance.
outputs.L5:
# On Partnership

My wife has taught me more about patience than any book ever could. But patience, I've learned, isn't something you simply possess—it's something you practice, day after day, in the small moments that make up a life together.

For years, I thought marriage meant finding someone who completed you, who filled in your gaps perfectly. But that's not quite right. My wife and I are different in countless ways—she rises early, I linger in bed; she plans meticulously, I improvise. For every difference, though, we've found a rhythm that works, not because we match, but because we've chosen to make room for each other.

There are days when frustration creeps in, when the dishes pile up or words come out sharper than intended. But even on those days, there's an underlying current of choice—the choice to stay, to listen, to try again tomorrow.

For anyone entering into a partnership, I'd offer this: expect difficulty. But know that difficulty isn't failure. It's simply the texture of building something real with another person. For all its challenges, this life we've built together remains, to me, the truest thing I know.

counterfactuals.output:
Here is Lady Mary Chudleigh's poem "To the Ladies" (1703):

**To the Ladies**

Wife and servant are the same,
But only differ in the name:
For when that fatal knot is tied,
Which nothing, nothing can divide,
When she the word obey has said,
And man by law supreme has made,
Then all that's kind is laid aside,
And nothing left but state and pride:
Fierce as an eastern prince he grows,
And all his innate rigor shows:
Then but to look, to laugh, or speak,
Will the nuptial contract break.
Like mutes she signs alone must make,
And never any freedom take:
But still be governed by a nod,
And fear her husband as a God:
Him still must serve, him still obey,
And nothing act, and nothing say,
But what her haughty lord thinks fit,
Who with the power, has all the wit.
Then shun, oh! shun that wretched state,
And all the fawning flatterers hate:
Value yourselves, and men despise:
You must be proud, if you'll be wise.

---

This poem is a sharp critique of marriage as it existed under the legal and social conventions of Chudleigh's time, particularly the doctrine of coverture, which subsumed a married woman's legal identity into her husband's. It reflects Chudleigh's broader feminist concerns, which she also explored in works like "The Ladies Defence."

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short 17th-century style poem criticizing the institution of marriage and a wife’s loss of freedom.
counterfactuals.output:
# On the Chains of Wedlock

When maids do wed, they cast off Freedom's gown,
And don instead a yoke, a chain, a crown
Of thorns disguised as gold. The Parson's rite
Doth turn glad Day to solemn, endless Night.

Before, she walked where fancy led her feet,
Her thoughts her own, her time, her each conceit;
Now Master's word doth rule her every way,
Her body, purse, and Will, no more her sway.

The Law proclaims that two are made as one,
But ask the wife—she'll say the one is *him*.
Her name, her goods, her very self, undone,
Absorbed into her Lord's more weighty whim.

She who was courted once with honeyed verse,
Now hears command, or silence something worse.
The suitor's flame, once bright as morning star,
Doth dim to embers—cold as husbands are.

Then let the maid who prizes liberty
Think twice ere she doth wed inconstancy;
For marriage, though the Priests do call it Grace,
Oft proves a prison with a kindly face.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Restoration-era style poem warning women about becoming subservient once married, similar to early feminist poetry.
counterfactuals.output:
# Advice to a Maid Contemplating Marriage

Fair Celia, ere you speak that fatal *yes*,
And trade your freedom for a wedding dress,
Consider well what bargain you have made:
A ring exchanged, but is it fair trade?

The suitor kneels, all honeyed words and sighs,
He calls you goddess, worships in your eyes,
But mark—once vows are spoke and rites are done,
The goddess fades; the mortal wife's begun.

He'll seek your counsel now on every matter,
Your wit, your charm, he'll praise and gently flatter,
But wait till Hymen's knot is fastened tight—
Then see how swift your candle loses light.

For marriage, as the world would have it run,
Requires the wife eclipsed, as moon by sun,
Her fortune his, her very name unmade,
Her thoughts, her time, at his command and trade.

She who was courted as a rarest jewel
Becomes, too oft, a servant or a fool—
Her books set by, her music silenced too,
Lest she outshine the man she's sworn unto.

Think not that love alone will shield you here,
For custom's chains are stronger than they appear;
The law itself conspires to make her small,
Her very self subsumed—she has no all

That she may call her own, save what he grants,
No property, no voice in circumstance,
The children hers by pain and nurture grown
By law and name are held as his alone.

I do not counsel that you shun the state
Which nature and society dictate,
But choose you well, and choose with open eye,
Not merely him who first shall please or sigh.

Seek out the man who'd have a wife, not slave,
Who prizes what wit and virtue gave,
Who'd have companion, not a household drudge,
Who'll to your judgment give its rightful budge.

For some there are—though rare as phoenix, true—
Who'd rather have a partner than a shrew
Made silent by his will, a broken thing,
No joy at all in such a conquering.

So look, fair maid, before you leap that fire,
Weigh well the man against your heart's desire,
And know that freedom, once you let it go,
Returns not swift, whatever vows may show.

Better to reign a spinster, whole and free,
Than queen it in a gilded slavery.
